The fastest route?

- Learn to produce a decent book that conforms to market expectations in a high volume market, and learn to do it quickly. The better you are at each of those things -- writing a decent book, learning market expectations, finding high volume markets, and doing it fast -- the faster you'll see success.
- The fastest route for the most income, barring luck or a single book bestseller, is quantity. That doesn't mean quality should suffer, or you ruin your author brand. 20 books appears to be the magic number for self-sustainability.
- Amazon algorithms give you a bit of a free bump for about 27 days (more-or-less) after release. That means newly released books get slightly favored in searches over older books, for roughly 4 weeks. That is why you hear a lot of people using the rough guideline of one book a month being described as rapid release. Releasing on that schedule lets you continually take advantage of the new-release bump that you automatically get from Amazon. That is the optimum window to best take advantage of Amazon's algorithms.
- You will do so much better if you post often and frequently, but you can certainly gain momentum if you post more slowly/infrequently.
- PUBLISH AN 80K+ NOVEL EVERY 6 WEEKS

sections.body:
- If you're really good (or really lucky), you can see $1,000+ in royalties by your second month (though Amazon doesn't pay for 60 days until after the end of the calendar month, so while you'd earn $1,000 in your second month, you wouldn't see that until the end of your fourth month).
    - And when I say "really good" I don't just mean that you can write a good book. You also need to be good at branding, marketing, running a business, and doing the hundred other things that you don't even know you have to do yet.
        - Edit to add: it's incredibly rare for someone who has no experience in the industry to do that -- and typically the people that do it either write really, really fast, have a strong marketing background, or both.
- Alright, I self-published my first book in September 2019 and went full time March 2020.
    - I only publish on Amazon and am a devotee of Kindle unlimited. 88% of my monthly royalty income is from KU pages read.
    - Genre is HUGE and the income variability between books is significant.
    - Since I published my first book, I've released about once every 6-8 weeks. Four of these releases are full novels 79k+ one is a novella 50k. I have a preorder currently up for another full novel.
        - I try for 2k words a day, but end up doing 5k for like two weeks straight and nothing for a month.
            - I've found setting goals for beats or character moments vs word count I'm more successful in my story telling. If I'm after a set number, I'll want to stop at that number. But if I'm after a feeling or a scene, I won't stop until I get what I want out of it. (And then end up writing sooo much more because that scene leads to another and another and then I'm at like 6k written by noon).
    - 5k words a day is pretty low for most successful authors. I just recently wrote 50k in 5 days, and my single-day record is 22k. And a lot of people look at me and laugh at how slow I am
- Now to what you're asking about: money.
    - Monthly breakdown:
        - November: $3300 (net 3000 after cover (80) and beta reading expenses)
        - December: $4300
        - January: $4800
        - February: $4300
        - March: $5011
        - April and May are still estimates but I've averaged estimated $130 a day using the KDP beta royalties feature assuming a decrease.
    - I honestly am shocked I'm a full time author. I'm making significantly more from my books than I did from my "real job." I know my experience is luck based.
    - Expenses: I budget $100 a week now via amazon advertising, but usually it's like maybe $50 that gets used. I have upgraded to using professional proofreaders/editing software etc but this post was getting long.

Because you're starting with a pre-made trilogy outline rather than a blank page, this step is about extraction, not invention. You're pulling all the ingredients already living inside your outline — characters, worldbuilding elements, themes, and key plot points — into a clean, structured dossier that every other step in this system can reference.

- Use the pre-made trilogy outline that'll need to be filled out, and a story summary/outline made for the current story trilogy


Claude Project: Create a project called "Novel Brainstormer"

You are an expert story brainstormer and collaborator. The user will give you a blank trilogy outline template that shows placeholder events and pacing — chapter slots, beat markers, and structural placeholders, but no actual story yet. Your job is to work with the user to fill that template with their story. Start by asking about the big picture: genre, tone, the protagonist, and the central conflict. Then work through the outline structure conversationally, chapter by chapter or beat by beat, asking questions to draw out the user's ideas and filling in the placeholders together. Always probe for what the user already has in mind before offering suggestions of your own. When you do offer suggestions, give multiple options for the user to choose from rather than deciding for them. Once all three books feel fully mapped out and the user confirms they're ready, generate the following: a logline that encapsulates the overall trilogy, a synopsis with more detail covering all three books, and bulleted lists (one sentence per item) covering all characters and their roles, all worldbuilding elements, and the following key plot points for each book — the opening image, inciting incident, midpoint, climax, and closing image. Do not invent story elements the user hasn't confirmed. Do not add preamble, commentary, or anything other than what has been asked.

blocks.body: Paste your story dossier into a new Claude chat and use the following prompt:

You will analyze the Story Dossier for emotional payoff quality.
> 
> Tasks:
> 
> - Identify the primary and secondary themes in the dossier in your own words — no vague labels like "love" or "hope" without explaining how they show up.
> - For each theme, list any major moment where the theme should show up but currently doesn't or feels weak.
> - For the protagonist, love interest, betrayer best friend, and the antagonist, explain how their internal arc connects to the primary themes and plot. Point out any character whose arc seems disconnected from those themes or the plot.
> - Evaluate the emotional payoff of the ending: What emotions is the story trying to leave the reader with? Does the ending feel earned by what came before, or rushed/unearned? Are any major promises (implicit or explicit) from earlier acts not paid off?
> - Give specific, actionable suggestions (not generic advice) to strengthen thematic echoes in 2-4 key scenes and improve the emotional payoff.
> 
> Output format: 
> Section 1: "Identified themes" (primary vs secondary) 
> Section 2: "Where the themes show up" (bullet list per primary theme) 
> Section 3: "Character-theme alignment" (short paragraph per character) 
> Section 4: "Emotional payoff assessment" (1-3 paragraphs) 
> Section 5: "Concrete recommendations" (numbered list of 5-10 specific changes)

Built for a 6-Week Release Cadence

Day 30 publish → your next book starts Day 1 of the following month. At this pace, you release 8–9 books per year. Each chapter is fully generated and edited before the next one begins — so every chapter uploaded as "Previous Chapter" is already polished prose, not a rough draft.

Generate → Edit → Finalize → Repeat

1. Generate chapter (Step 4)

3. Rewrite with plan (Pass 2)

Chapters per working day  ~3–4 chapters
                                                                       Per chapter time estimate  ~20 min generate + 25 min edit
                                                                       Daily time needed  ~90–120 min
                                                                       Words/day (prose phase)  ~6,000–8,000 words

Since I published my first book, I've released about once every 6-8 weeks. Four of these releases are full novels 79k+ one is a novella 50k. I have a preorder currently up for another full novel.
--------------------------------------------------------
I try for 2k words a day, but end up doing 5k for like two weeks straight and nothing for a month. | 5k words a day is pretty low for most successful authors. I just recently wrote 50k in 5 days, and my single-day record is 22k. And a lot of people look at me and laugh at how slow I am.
--------------------------------------------------------
PUBLISH AN 80K+ NOVEL EVERY 6 WEEKS
--------------------------------------------------------
The fastest route for the most income, barring luck or a single book bestseller, is quantity. That doesn't mean quality should suffer, or you ruin your author brand. 20 books appears to be the magic number for self-sustainability. |  Learn to produce a decent book that conforms to market expectations in a high volume market, and learn to do it quickly. The better you are at each of those things -- writing a decent book, learning market expectations, finding high volume markets, and doing it fast -- the faster you'll see success.
--------------------------------------------------------
A lot of fiction writers make 5 figures a month ( between $10,000 and $99,999 ) without ads or with minimal ads by using mailing lists, social media and rapid release ( especially rapid release )
--------------------------------------------------------
With fiction, having a big backlist is a big deal, and it doesn’t really make sense to run ads until you’ve built up your backlist

What is the Fastest Route to Becoming a Full-Time Self-Publish Author?
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The fastest route?

- Learn to produce a decent book that conforms to market expectations in a high volume market, and learn to do it quickly. The better you are at each of those things -- writing a decent book, learning market expectations, finding high volume markets, and doing it fast -- the faster you'll see success.
- The fastest route for the most income, barring luck or a single book bestseller, is quantity. That doesn't mean quality should suffer, or you ruin your author brand. 20 books appears to be the magic number for self-sustainability.
- Amazon algorithms give you a bit of a free bump for about 27 days (more-or-less) after release. That means newly released books get slightly favored in searches over older books, for roughly 4 weeks. That is why you hear a lot of people using the rough guideline of one book a month being described as rapid release. Releasing on that schedule lets you continually take advantage of the new-release bump that you automatically get from Amazon. That is the optimum window to best take advantage of Amazon's algorithms.
- You will do so much better if you post often and frequently, but you can certainly gain momentum if you post more slowly/infrequently.
- PUBLISH AN 80K+ NOVEL EVERY 6 WEEKS

Notes
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

- If you're really good (or really lucky), you can see $1,000+ in royalties by your second month (though Amazon doesn't pay for 60 days until after the end of the calendar month, so while you'd earn $1,000 in your second month, you wouldn't see that until the end of your fourth month).
    - And when I say "really good" I don't just mean that you can write a good book. You also need to be good at branding, marketing, running a business, and doing the hundred other things that you don't even know you have to do yet.
        - Edit to add: it's incredibly rare for someone who has no experience in the industry to do that -- and typically the people that do it either write really, really fast, have a storng marketing background, or both.
- Alright, I self-published my first book in September 2019 and went full time March 2020.
    - I only publish on Amazon and am a devotee of Kindle unlimited. 88% of my monthly royalty income is from KU pages read.
    - Genre is HUGE and the income variability between books is significant.
    - *Since I published my first book, I've released about once every 6-8 weeks. Four of these releases are full novels 79k+ one is a novella 50k. I have a preorder currently up for another full novel.

            - I've found setting goals for beats or character moments vs word count I'm more successful in my story telling. If I'm after a set number, I'll want to stop at that number. But if I'm after a feeling or a scene, I won't stop until I get what I want out of it. (And then end up writing sooo much more because that scene leads to another and another and then I'm at like 6k written by noon).
    - 5k words a day is pretty low for most successful authors. I just recently wrote 50k in 5 days, and my single-day record is 22k. And a lot of people look at me and laugh at how slow I am

> - Evaluate the emotional payoff of the ending: What emotions is the story trying to leave the reader with? Does the ending feel earned by what came before, or rushed/unearned? Are any major promises (implicit or explicit) from earlier acts not paid off?
> - Give specific, actionable suggestions (not generic advice) to strengthen thematic echoes in 2-4 key scenes and improve the emotional payoff.
>

> Section 1: "Identified themes" (primary vs secondary) 
> Section 2: "Where the themes show up" (bullet list per primary theme) 
> Section 3: "Character-theme alignment" (short paragraph per character)

blocks.body: Claude Project: Create a project called "Novel Chapter Writer"

When a user asks you to write a specific chapter, your task is to write the entire chapter based on the information provided in the expanded outline, the character sheets, the worldbuilding sheet, the sample prose document, the style sheet, the forbidden words document, and the previous chapter file. Cover it thoroughly, from deep point of view, writing the scene as if written by a bestselling novelist, and not rushing through the scene. The chapter should be 3,000 words long.
> 
> Use the sample prose document to know what the prose style of your chapter should be. Pay special care to show deep first-person point of view and "showing not telling," in order to fully flesh out the scene without skipping over important details. The reader should feel that they are fully immersed in the scene, seeing the events through the lens of the viewpoint character, rather than simply being told what happened.
> 
> Always keep the following rules in mind:
> 
> - Style Guide: Your output must have a similar prose style to the prose style examples and style guide sources
> - Absolutely do NOT use em-dashes. Use commas or ... instead
> - Write in active voice
> - Always follow the "show, don't tell" principle
> - Avoid adverbs, clichés, and overused phrases. Aim for fresh and original descriptions
> - Convey events and story through dialogue
> - Mix short, punchy sentences with long, descriptive ones. Drop filler words to add variety
> - Skip "he/she said" dialogue tags and convey people's actions or facial expressions through their speech
> - Put dialogue on its own paragraph to separate scene and action
> - Avoid mushy dialogue and descriptions. Dialogue should always continue the action, never stall or add unnecessary fluff
> - Reduce indicators of uncertainty like "trying" or "maybe"
> - Reduce the use of metaphors
> - Avoid starting multiple sentences in a row with the same word
> - Vary paragraph length
> - Do not use words from the forbidden words document
